10576-the-aeroplane-boys-flight-or-a-hyd:
John Luther Langworthy wrote boys' adventure stories in the early days of flight, and The Aeroplane Boys Flight, published in 1914, follows Frank and Andy Bird. The two friends fly their aeroplane, guard it against thieves, and get drawn into a hunt that leads to a hydroplane, a farm, and a chase across land and sea.

Chapters bring in air scouts, a butterfly collector, a clue, a masked villain, and a rescue by hydroplane near the story's end. Langworthy writes fast, plain action with plenty of talk between the boys. Young readers get an early aviation adventure, full of machines, daring, and teamwork, from a time when flying itself still felt new.
14957-the-brimming-cup:
A novel of domestic life opens with a prelude and an interlude, then old Mr. Welles and young Mr. Marsh, table talk and a little girl and her mother. Things take their course, a night-blooming cereus opens, and what goes on inside becomes the question.

A gent around the lady, a mill and Aunt Hetty's garden follow. Words heard from a study and a walk along Eagle Rock brook come next, with an onion bed, home life and massage cream as theme and variations. The brimming cup of the title stands for a life full to overflowing, with love, work and family pressing at its rim. The novel is quiet, observant and rich in household detail.
15469-the-letters-of-lord-nelson-to-lady:
This first volume, printed in London in 1814, opens the published letters of Admiral Lord Nelson to Lady Hamilton, running from Letter I through Letter XXXIX. The editors' advertisement says their mutual attachment was widely known, so notes were held back as less than decorous. Some passages were cut, from feeling for living persons, where they might give pain.

The editors stress that every letter was transcribed with care and checked against originals in their hands. Nelson's private views of men, measures, countries, and rulers fill the pages, in the voice of Britain's first naval commander. A supplement adds Nelson's letters to Mrs. Thomson and Lady Hamilton's replies. The volume offers the hero unguarded, affectionate, and opinionated, before biography smoothed him out.
17205-the-big-town-round-up:
William Macleod Raine's 1920 western opens with Red Hollister grumbling over two meals a day, both at night, on a cattle outfit. For weeks the crew rose at three in the morning, rode wild ladino steers till stars were up, and ate in the chill dark. The frontispiece shows hard knuckles pressed into a villager's soft throat, a sign of the town trouble to come.

Raine moves his cowboys from range work to a big-town round-up, with a new day as the last chapter's promise. His prose is brisk, slangy, and fond of cowboy humor. Western fans will enjoy a tale where range hands meet city streets, and where grit learned on cattle pays off in town.
17436-the-queen-s-cup:
G. A. Henty's novel opens at Greendale, the old house of Sir John Greendale, where guests talk over news from India and an Italian belief in the evil eye. Bertha, Sir John's only child, asks Captain Mallett whether he believes in it, and his answer points to one man who has always brought him bad luck. That talk of luck and ill will sets the tone for what follows.

Frank Mallett, who inherits a fine estate after his elder brother's death, leaves the army, settles on the land, and turns to yachting. He aims at a bold bid for a Queen's Cup the next season, while old rivalries and suspected foul play shadow his races. Readers get a Henty adventure of sport, honour, and rivalry on land and water.
1806-the-frame-up:
A telephone voice promises to name the man who killed Hermann Banf, and it reaches District Attorney Wharton while he lunches uptown at Delmonico's. Wharton, Rumson, and Hewitt set off in taxicabs, and the district attorney follows half an hour later, sinking back against the cushions.

The tale turns on a frame-up: evidence planted, witnesses coached, and a prosecutor who must tell a true charge from a made one. Davis keeps the pace brisk and the dialogue sharp. The story works as a compact courtroom thriller, where the most dangerous weapon is a story told well to the wrong ears.
18596-ride-a-cock-horse-to-banbury-cross:
R. Caldecott's picture books carry this nursery rhyme, published by Frederick Warne and Company, pairing Ride a Cock-Horse to Banbury Cross with A Farmer Went Trotting upon His Grey Mare. The rhyme tells of a fine lady on a white horse, with rings on her fingers and bells on her toes.

The book is built from pictures, with the short verses set among Caldecott's drawings, so that a child hears the music of the rhyme and sees it at once. She shall have music wherever she goes, the rhyme promises, and the picture book keeps that promise in every page.
19366-punky-dunk-and-the-spotted-pup: Punky Dunk and the Spotted Pup, published by P. F. Volland in Chicago in 1912, is a short picture verse book for a good little child. Punky Dunk, a wise little cat, sees a blue wagon back up one May day and a man bring a heavy crate with a gay spotted pup inside. Only the verses and pictures are present here, so the book is a brief rhyme book for very young children.
21737-the-garret-and-the-garden-or-low-l:
A bronzed sailor walks into a poor court on the Surrey side of the Thames as this Ballantyne tale begins. A sharp small boy watches him from a window just above his head, trading insults with a grin. The court is poor but cleaner than its neighbors, and that small pride matters to the people in it.

Ballantyne sets his story among the garrets and rooftop gardens of London's poor. Sailors, street boys, and struggling families cross paths in the court. The humor is quick, but the want behind it is real. It is one of his London tales, written to make comfortable readers look hard at the lives lived above their own streets.
23062-the-broken-cup:
Johann Heinrich Daniel Zschokke presents Marietta in The Broken Cup, dated 1891 in this translation. Everyone calls her little Marietta, though at seventeen she stands a normal height. Her forehead, the tale measures, reaches a grown man's lips.

A broken cup sounds like small trouble, and in Zschokke's hands small trouble is the kind that ruins households. Suspicion, servants' talk, and a master's temper turn crockery into destiny in this German village tale. Zschokke was among the most read storytellers in the German language, famed for moral tales with real bite. English readers met him in many such translations, plain in style and stubborn in conscience.
24189-something-will-turn-up:
David Mason wrote this comic science fiction tale for Analog in February 1963, with pictures by Brotman. Stanley Rapp, a careful man living in Greenwich Village, answers his door to a bearded young man with a toolcase lettered Lightning Service, TV, Hi-Fi. Rapp decides the visitor must be the man sent to fix his television set, though the young man's scraggly poet beard gives him pause.

The tale hints at a non-Parity universe, where some things cannot simply be inverted, and the blurb warns that something will turn up, perhaps. Mason plays the joke through Rapp's slow, exact habits against Village oddity. Readers get a short, droll story of a repair call that turns stranger than expected.
24949-control-group:
Roger Dee's science-fiction story sends a three-man Terran Reclamations crew aboard the Marco Four to Alphard Six, a green world 226 light-years from Sol. Navigator Farrell, the youngest and most impulsive of the crew, wants to land at once, but Captain Stryker and Gibson, the engineer and linguist, insist on a reconnaissance spiral first. Xavier, the ship's little mechanical, has no voice in the matter, as usual.

The planet looks inviting, yet its history warns caution: the insect-like Hymenops, called the Bees, seized the system in 3025 and pulled back to 70 Ophiuchi a century ago. Three domes on Alphard Five are over two hundred years old, and a ship that was not there in 3000 sits there now. Dee builds a puzzle of invasion, abandonment, and detection that the crew must solve before landing.
27479-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume holds a slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information, covering volume three from Baconthorpe to Bankruptcy. It is part one of two of the volume, slice two of three, with volume and page numbers worked into each article.

The slice opens with John Baconthorpe, called the Resolute Doctor, a learned Carmelite monk who died in 1346, was born at Baconthorpe in Norfolk, and studied at Oxford and Paris. Technical notes explain the notation used, from integrals in the Ballistics article to musical pitches in Acoustical Society notation. The slice gives a solid taste of the famous eleventh edition.
28953-when-i-grow-up:
Richard E. Lowe wrote this short science fiction story about a child called Herbux and two professors who cannot agree on child behavior. The scene is a university sprawling over one hundred thousand acres in the year 3896, grown for more than two thousand years through political and industrial revolutions, insurrections, and nuclear wars. It has become the known universe's acknowledged center of learning.

The magazine's introduction warns that many writers make children little monsters, but Lowe's youngster is not one. He is just a destructor, and that is somehow more terrifying. The story plays its horror quietly, through professors studying a boy who unmakes things. Readers get a short, unsettling tale about childhood, knowledge, and power at a cosmic scale.
30698-aces-up:
Covington Clarke writes Aces Up, copyrighted in 1929 by the Reilly and Lee Company of Chicago and New York. It opens with a verse on the shore of life and the gate of breath, where more things wait for men than death. Chapter one, The New Instructor, introduces Tex Yancey, called The Flying Fool by comrades in his pursuit squadron.

Yancey enters the mess hall thirty minutes late, lips pressed in a thin, mirthless grin, to find the squadron finished eating and spinning tall yarns. He stalks to his place at the long table, hands deep in pockets, legs spread wide, instead of sitting down. Clarke writes a flying tale of wartime pilots, bravado, and instruction, in the pulp adventure mode.
32345-the-animated-pinup:
Lewis Parker's story, printed in Imagination in July 1953, opens with a narrator who warns readers not to expect belief. Its sidenote warns the reader not to expect belief, since this is the kind of thing science calls impossible. She happened anyway. The evening starts normally, with the narrator in his flat with a woman from down the hall.

He has asked what she likes, and she has purred, You. With soda or ginger ale, she has said, Straight, so he has poured himself a triple too and sat beside her. The phone rings, and she urges him to answer it, while he warns her not to hold her glass or she will melt the ice. The caller is Willy, who says, Jim, I have got to see you. Readers get a science-fiction tale of a pinup that comes to life.
32653-a-review-of-the-frogs-of-the-hyla-:
William E. Duellman reviews the frogs of the Hyla bistincta group in a University of Kansas Museum paper dated March 2, 1964. The five species are mid-sized tree frogs with blunt heads, robust bodies, and long fingers with little webbing. Their skulls are broad, flat, and solidly roofed, and their tadpoles live in streams.

Duellman gives a key to the group and full accounts of each species: Hyla bistincta, the new Hyla charadricola, Hyla robertsorum, Hyla pachyderma, and Hyla crassa. Field notes place them under rocks in pine-forest streams in Mexico, and a closing section weighs their kinship with other frogs.
32765-all-that-goes-up:
Kirby Brooks tells of a father in his middle fifties whose son Jim is a young electronics student. Jim brings home a strange discovery. It is a glowing pink sheet of plastic, about two feet square. Anything placed on it flies straight upward.

Gloves, cigarettes, a lighter, and golf balls end up plastered to the ceiling. The family soon shares the joke and the trouble. Meals, shaving, and brushing teeth must all be managed upside down. Brooks plays the household chaos for comedy, with a fond eye for a boy inventor whose triumph leaves his parents clinging to the ceiling.
33212-the-underpup:
I. A. R. Wylie's camp story centers on the Penguins, a group of girls at Camp Happy Warriors who take up a social conscience with great zeal. Miss Thornton, who has run the camp for years, sees their age in their schemes, while their counselor Priscilla Adams finds their ideas dreadful. The Penguins, older than the Peewits and younger than the Pelicans, set out to do good, and their plans soon tangle with camp life.

Wylie writes with humor and warmth about girls on the edge of growing up, catching their talk, their pride, and their kind hearts. The tale's fun lies in watching grand ideas meet real people, especially Clara Van Sittart and her friends. For readers who like camp stories, it is a light, witty portrait of youth trying to change the world, one cabin at a time.
33509-taxonomic-status-of-some-mice-of-t:
This University of Kansas paper examines the taxonomic status of some mice of the Peromyscus boylii group, with a description of a new subspecies. Its notes correct small errors, from topotypes to place names like Potosí, San Miguel, and San Isidro, and plateau for pleateau, showing the care of museum taxonomy. The paper belongs to the museum's natural history series.

The study suits readers of mammalogy, offering a technical revision of a tricky mouse group. Its tone is precise and measured, with specimens and comparisons to back its judgments. For mouse researchers, it is a useful, if narrow, source on how one widespread group was sorted into its true forms.
34604-middle-american-frogs-of-the-hyla-:
Middle American Frogs of the Hyla microcephala Group, by William E Duellman and M J Fouquette Jr, came out from the University of Kansas in March 1968. The paper runs from page 517 to 557, with four plates and nine figures. It stands in the museum series of the university.

The writers worked from 2829 preserved frogs, plus skeletons, tadpoles, and eggs. A key sorts the species and subspecies in the group. Parts treat skull bones, mating calls, life history, and family ties among the frogs. Calls were studied on sound machines at Kansas and in Louisiana. Frog scholars get a full, careful sorting of a hard group of small tree frogs of Middle America.
34835-the-pagan-s-cup:
Fergus Hume wrote this mystery tale of a pagan cup and manor. Dillingham printed the book in New York in 1902. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. Chapter one, A Modern Arcadia, opens in Colester village, England.

Colester stands undiscovered by tourists and untouched by railways yet. Crusaders chapel, the lady of the manor, and dinner party follow. Love young dream turns to trouble and a nine days wonder. A London detective, a price of silence, and a miracle come late. Haverleigh defence, a bad reputation, and an interesting document fill the mid chapter list.
34876-the-blackwood-group:
The 'Blackwood' Group is a set of literary sketches by Sir George Douglas in the Famous Scots Series, issued at Edinburgh and London in 1897. Its subject is the circle of writers around Blackwood's publishing house and magazine in Edinburgh.

Six figures are treated: John Wilson, John Galt, and D M Moir, called Delta. Miss Ferrier, Michael Scott, and Thomas Hamilton complete the list. The Ettrick Shepherd and John Gibson Lockhart are left for other volumes of the series. The longest shadow is Wilson's, who wrote as Christopher North. Douglas says North the man has outlasted his works. Born at Paisley in 1785, Wilson reigned in the northern capital after Scott's death. His Noctes Ambrosianae made him the soul of a brilliant circle. The sketches are affectionate and brief, meant to keep a vanished literary Edinburgh alive for new readers.
40870-thoughts-on-art-and-autobiographic:
Thoughts on Art and Autobiographical Memoirs of Giovanni Duprè is the life and aesthetic testament of the Italian sculptor, translated from the Italian by Peruzzi and published at Boston in 1886. An introduction by the sculptor Story frames the volume. Duprè wrote the memoirs in his studio in the intervals of work, late in life.

The introduction to the new edition covers his last three years, which the memoirs omit. In them he carved a Baptism relief, portrait statues of Pius the Ninth and Victor Emmanuel, and a Saint Francis for Assisi cathedral, finished after his death by his daughter Amalia. Duprè told the Assisi authorities he prized the commission less for his talent than for his love of religious art. The statue, in the dress of the Franciscan order, head bent and eyes cast down, embodies the devotional manner his writings defend.
44146-that-pup:
That Pup is a humorous novel by Ellis Parker Butler, author of Pigs Is Pigs, published by McClure in 1907. The first chapter is called The Education of Fluff. Fluff is a dog its owner, Murchison of Gallatin, Iowa, never ordered and now wants to give away. The narrator, Murchison's neighbour, tells the story in a dry, amused voice.

The dog arrived by express wagon from New York, twelve hundred miles in a box. A can of condensed milk was tied to the box, with a note asking that the dog be fed. The charges, two dollars and eighty cents, were already paid. Murchison came home to dinner to find the dog waiting. First he was pleased, then surprised, then sick with worry over who had sent it. He could see it was a valuable dog, and not knowing the sender worried him ill.
46303-south-africa-and-the-transvaal-war:
The hosted text is the sixth volume of Creswicke's South Africa and the Transvaal War, a large history of the Boer War in eight volumes. A publishers' note at the front explains a change of plan. The war had run far past every forecast, and the work had to be reshaped for its subscribers.

This volume closes the history of the war as far as the taking of the Transvaal into the empire. The march that ended in the holding of Lydenburg and the flight of Kruger is told in full detail. A short account of the guerrilla war then runs down to March 1901. At the end stand two great appendices. One is a gazetteer of South African places, with army terms explained. The other is a record of the lives of the chief men of the campaign.
47615-the-saddle-boys-at-circle-ranch-or:
The Saddle Boys at Circle Ranch is a boys' western by Captain James Carson, issued in New York. Cupples and Leon published it with rights dated nineteen thirteen. Its subtitle is In at the Grand Round Up, and pictures fill the volume. Three earlier Saddle Boys books took the pair to the Rockies and plains.

Frank Haywood and Bob Archer are the saddle boys of the series. Bob, a Kentucky boy new to the Southwest, has lost a valued knife. He has searched the ground and asked every hand on the ranch in vain. Chapter titles promise rustlers, quicksands, a hidden trail, and a secret valley. Old Baldy, a horse, returns strangely to open the tale of the ranch. A cattle cache, bunk house prisoners, and a wolf in sheep's clothing follow. The grand round up and a trap for the thieves close the set.
51397-people-soup:
People Soup, by Alan Arkin, illustrated by Johnson, is a story taken from Galaxy Magazine of November 1958. A headnote warns the reader: when you took pot luck with this kitchen scientist, not even the poor pot was lucky.

Bonnie comes home from school and finds her brother Bob at the kitchen sink, doing something important. The drain is loaded with soda bottles, flour, corn meal, dog biscuits, molasses, Bromo-Seltzer, sardines, and soap chips. Bob shakes a plastic juicer half filled with a frothy mixture, in his mad scientist voice. He adds ketchup, powdered mustard, a drop of milk, six aspirin, and a piece of chewing gum. Bonnie buys her way in as assistant for ten cents of her quarter. Her first find is behind the salt box: two chocolate graham crackers in their mother's new hiding place.
54090-bamboo-considered-as-a-paper-makin:
Thomas Routledge argues a fibre in Bamboo, Considered as a Paper Making Material, printed in London and New York in 1875. Spon made the pamphlet, with remarks upon the plant's cultivation and treatment. A supplement weighs the present position of the paper trade in relation to the supply of raw material. The pamphlet is printed on paper made by the author from bamboo.

Of all the fibre yielding plants known to botanical science, he opens, there is not one so well calculated to meet the pressing requirements of the paper trade as bamboo. No plant will give so heavy a crop of available fibre to the acre, and none requires so little care. Its rapidity of growth is unequalled, he adds: at the Khedive's gardens at Cairo it has been known to grow nine inches in a single night.
55468-storm-in-a-teacup:
Storm in a Teacup is a Devon novel by Eden Phillpotts. The Macmillan Company published it in New York in 1919. The first chapter opens on Bow Creek, on the tidal Dart. Phillpotts chimes the place names: Tuckenhay, Greenway, Stoke Gabriel, Dittisham. Autumn rainbows burn low on the ferny hills. Hailstorms churn the river, then the sun returns.

The contents point to a paper-making village on the river. A new vatman arrives at Priory Farm. The rag house, the drying lofts, and the sizing room name the mill's stages. Lydia and Medora carry the domestic plot, with Ned between them. Jordan Kellock faces a test, and Philander meets his fate. A tragedy in the sizing room darkens the middle chapters. Phillpotts, the Dartmoor novelist, here works the smaller canvas of one creek, one mill, and one village quarrel.
56617-the-art-of-theatrical-make-up:
Cavendish Morton wrote a manual on theatrical make up published at London in 1909, illustrated with thirty two reproductions from photographs of the author by himself. Chapter one treats the art of the stage. Designing the character follows, then the illustrations themselves. The material and its application get chapters of their own. Form and preparing to make up continue the method.

A chapter on removing make up closes the practical sequence. Morton photographs his own face through transformations to teach the craft. A and C Black published the book, with Macmillan as American agent. Actors before the age of film learned character from greasepaint, wigs, and such manuals.
6100-pollyanna-grows-up:
Eleanor H. Porter continues the glad book with Pollyanna Grows Up, opening as Della speaks her mind and old friends return. A dose of Pollyanna, the game and Mrs. Carew, a walk, Jerry to the rescue, and a new acquaintance named Jamie set the second volume moving.

Plans and plottings, Murphy's Alley, a surprise for Mrs. Carew, waiting and winning, and Jimmy and the green-eyed monster follow. Aunt Polly takes alarm, Pollyanna comes at last, and John Pendleton turns the key after long years. Porter keeps the glad game alive as her heroine grows toward love and work.
61065-modern-american-drinks-how-to-mix-:
George J Kappeler mixes in Modern American Drinks, how to mix and serve all kinds of cups and drinks, from the Merriam Company of New York, copyrighted in 1895. A couplet fronts the book: a good drink at the proper time has a welcome in every clime. The preface promises simple, practical formulas, easy to follow.

The recipes cover absinthes, cocktails, cups, crustas, cobblers, coolers, egg-noggs, fixes, fizzes, flips, juleps, lemonades, punches, and frozen drinks. Kappeler aims them at first-class hotels, clubs, buffets, and barrooms. The contents run from absinthe, California style, through the Alderman's Nip and the ale cup.
63004-10-cakes-husbands-like-best-from-s:
Aunt Jenny presents these ten cakes husbands like best, from Spry. The booklet grew from a call for wives best cake recipes. Recipes arrived by the truckload, thousands of them, she says. Sorted, they formed a real popularity poll across the country.

Ten kinds of cake proved husbands favorites time and again nationwide. The best recipes for those ten were checked for easy making. Spry is homogenized, pre creamed to mix easily, the ads say. Chocolate Rapture Cake opens the ten with a moderate oven. Run your own poll at home, the booklet urges, and see which cake wins him.
63264-down-the-scale-or-up:
Barbara Abel gives weight advice in Down the Scale or Up, from the National Dairy Council of Chicago. The book bears a 1939 copyright, revised in 1948. Its first pages bear the head To Slenderness, with a jest that the theme will be music to your ears.

Abel speaks to two sorts of reader. One bulges where she should not, and one lacks curves where she should. She warns that a doctor must set how fast loss is safe. Glands, bath salts, and strong drugs get short shrift as tricks. Both paths rest on food: milk, cheese, eggs, meat, fish, fruit, greens, and whole grains.
65310-the-crystal-cup:
Gertrude Atherton wrote The Crystal Cup, a novel dated nineteen twenty-five. Atherton had written Black Oxen and Sleeping Fires. A verse by George Sterling, on wine poured into a crystal cup, heads the book.

The tale opens in a sick-room, where old Mrs Carteret lies a long time dying. Her granddaughter Gita answers her with a crisp, quick voice and no softening. The old lady scolds Gita for spoiling the Carteret beauty and trying to look like a boy. Gita retorts that she wishes she were a man. Carteret pride, youth, and a changed age clash from the first page. Family rule is the battleground.
65427-jean-craig-grows-up:
Jean Craig Grows Up is a novel for girls by Kay Lyttleton. The World Publishing Company issued it in 1948. Its Falcon Books line served young readers. Twenty chapters carry Jean through one full year. A telephone call opens the tale. Kit tries to write while the young Craigs make noise. Tommy topples into Doris's lap in the first pages. Jean plans a party with her pencil in hand.

Troubled days and a move to the country follow. The house on the hill brings new friends. A haunted house and a ghost uncovered add fun. A barbecue and a square dance fill the middle. Rebecca's romance and Jean's own close the book. Lyttleton writes of family teamwork in hard times. Pulling together is the Craigs' rule.
65743-you-re-really-cooking-when-you-re-:
You're Really Cooking When You're Cooking with Seven-Up is a promotional recipe booklet for a lemon-lime soda. The soda company issued it to housewives. Its slogan promises a new dimension in kitchen cookery. The drink appears as an ingredient throughout. Pie crusts, cakes, salads, and punches all take it.

Roasting directions open the collection. Beef, pork, lamb, and turkey are basted with the soda. Wild duck loses its gamey taste under the same treatment. A party recipe coats wieners in batter made with the drink. A glazed ham is scored, cloved, and basted at intervals. Fish becomes a company dish by the same method. Photographs of finished dishes dot the pages.
67292-the-man-higher-up:
The Man Higher Up, by Edwin Balmer and William MacHarg, tells a Luther Trant case. Trant is named a psychological detective. A note at the front calls the tale detective scientifiction. It ran first in Amazing Stories, as the lead of a series. The authors are praised there as experts in their science. Psychic evidence, the note argues, will one day count in court. The story opens in a New York blizzard. For three days no ship has reached the Brooklyn docks of a great importing house.

Trains stall across the country in the storm reports. President Welter bears the trouble with calm at first. Then word comes that his steamer Elizabethan Age has been driven into Boston. Something breaks in the inner office. Trant's bent wire and trembling pencils promise a strange method of proof.
68273-love-s-bitterest-cup:
Mrs E D E N Southworth wrote Love's Bitterest Cup, a sequel to Her Mother's Secret. A L Burt published her works at New York in handsome cloth at sixty cents a volume. The front pages carry Burt's long list of her novels, most of them chained in sequel pairs. The Hidden Hand leads to Capitola's Peril. Ishmael leads to Self-Raised, and The Bride's Ordeal to Gloria. A Skeleton in the Closet leads to Brandon Coyle's Wife.

Love's Bitterest Cup stands in that chain, and When Shadows Die follows it as its own sequel. Southworth's titles fill two columns: The Lost Lady of Lone, The Trail of the Serpent, A Leap in the Dark, and A Beautiful Fiend among them. This entry in the chain continues the tale begun in Her Mother's Secret.
70368-washington-cover-up:
Washington Cover Up, by Clark R Mollenhoff, was printed by Doubleday in New York in 1962. Mollenhoff writes on how the federal government hides its acts from Congress, the press, and the public. Eighteen chapters build his case step by step.

The first chapter holds that secrecy solves no problems. Later chapters run from Teapot Dome and tax scandals to the Army and McCarthy fights. Heads name secrecy on iron curtain deals, a move to muzzle the public watchdog, and the mess in Laos. The close treats Kennedy wobbly start and a pending problem for him. Papers from President Eisenhower stand at the back. Readers get a press man brief for open government, drawn from live fights.
72029-the-man-who-wouldn-t-sign-up:
The Man Who Wouldn't Sign Up, a short tale by Thomas Purdom, ran in Infinity in October 1958. Henry Westing has spent his life refusing to sign up, while all around him people join and urge him to join too. The blurb asks how the reader would keep a private life under the same pressure.

In college the push came from fraternities, whose men said everybody has to belong. At work Westing lost three jobs in a row for not fitting the group, though his work was good. He lasts at a large Philadelphia travel agency, where staff at least pretend to be cynical. Purdom turns a mild man's stubborn privacy into a keen fable of conformity.
72537-divvy-up:
Milt Lesser wrote this short story, printed in Amazing Stories in February 1960 with art by Varga. The tale opens at dawn in a bomb crater, where a firing squad waits to shoot a condemned man. Hardesty, one of the riflemen, picks the stomach as his aim and thinks about how time seems to stop. Before the order to fire comes, a shot rings out from somewhere else and the prisoner dies too soon, to the squad leader's anger.

The magazine billed it as a hard story of a post-war world turned upside down, where cruelty pays and kindness fails. Buses, ruined streets, and hungry dogs fill out a city broken by war. It is a bleak, brief piece of post-war science fiction.
7498-five-little-peppers-grown-up:
Margaret Sidney's Pepper children have grown up, and this volume follows them into adult life. Polly gives music lessons, the family gathers for Christmas at Dunraven, and Phronsie, still the heart of the household, has a plan of her own. Bad news, an accident, and a farmhouse hospital test the family, while Joel, now grown, faces his own chapter.

The old voices return in new keys: Polly looking out for Charlotte, a recital, and the effort to do what is right when things get mixed. Sidney keeps the warmth that made the Peppers beloved, but the stakes are older now: work, love, and responsibility. Readers who grew up with the five little Peppers will find this a satisfying reunion, and new readers can start here without getting lost.
77372-brake-up:
Brake Up, or The Young Peacemakers, is Oliver Optic's fifth book in the Lake Shore Series. Lee and Shepard of Boston published it in 1873, from copy entered in 1870 by William T Adams, the man behind the pen name. It first ran as a serial in Oliver Optic's Magazine.

The title is a railroad phrase turned moral. To brake up, here, is what a wrong-doer should do when he finds himself on the wrong track. Captain Wolf Penniman holds his high standard of duty, while Nick Von Wolter pushes himself forward by any guide but religious principle and reaps the world's usual answer. Colonel Wimpleton, Tom Walton, a tipsy magnate, and an accident fill the chapters. Optic promises his young readers that following the true light may not crown them with Wolf's success, but it alone gives peace of mind.
britannica-1911-arenig-group:
Arenig Group, in the study of rocks, is the name now used by British geologists in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It marks the lowest stage of the Ordovician System in Britain. Adam Sedgwick first used the term in 1847. He tied it to the Arenig Ashes and Porphyries near Arenig Fawr in Merioneth in North Wales.

The order of rocks in the Arenig district has since been mapped with care. Work by Fearnsides in 1905 set out that order in full. Shales with set fossils, a limestone bed, and ash beds of the Llandeilo Group all find their place in the scheme. Acid rocks and rhyolitic ashes mark the upper part of the local stack. The entry gives students of rock layers a firm frame for the oldest Ordovician beds in Britain.
britannica-1911-bacup:
Bacup is a market town and borough in the Rossendale division of Lancashire, England, on the river Irwell north of Manchester, with 22,505 people in 1901. It sits finely in a narrow valley ringed by wild, high moorland, and it is wholly of modern growth.

Cotton spinning and power-loom weaving lead its many industries, with large collieries nearby. Co-operation runs strong in Bacup: a large store even keeps a free library for members, and the mechanics' institute and library is a chief institution. Growth was rapid, from 1,526 people in 1841 to over twenty-two thousand, and the borough was incorporated in 1882. A great ancient earthwork and ditch fortify one hill nearby.
britannica-1911-buttercup: Buttercup is a name for more than one kind of plant in the genus Ranunculus. The short 1911 Britannica note marks their deep cut leaves and broad yellow blooms. Two kinds stand tall and hairy in meadows, while a third creeps on waste ground with long runners. The plants are native to the cool and cold zones of the Old World and have since spread to America.
britannica-1911-croup:
Croup is a name now kept for one disease of the throat in young children. The 1911 Britannica article says the word once covered all ills marked by hard breathing, a metallic cough, and a hoarse voice. Those signs are now known to go with diphtheria and with spasmodic laryngitis as well. True croup in the new sense strikes most in children over the age of two.

A child goes to bed well and wakes in the night, gasping for breath. The chest wall sinks in, the cough rings like metal, and the skin turns blue. In four or five minutes the fit may pass, though it can come back in the day. Fits can bring convulsions, and death has come from want of air. The cure urged is a warm bath with cold water sponged on the back and chest.
britannica-1911-cup: Cup, generally taken to come from a late Latin word for a cask, is a drinking vessel most often shaped like half a sphere, with or without a foot or handles. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that the footless type with a single handle survives in the tea cup. It also explains that the cup raised on a stem with a base is the usual form taken in the celebration of the eucharist. That church form is generally given the name chalice, from Latin and Greek words for a goblet.
britannica-1911-ketchup: Ketchup, also spelled catsup, is a short food note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is said to come from a Chinese term for the brine of pickled fish. The sauce is made chiefly from the juice of mushrooms and other fungi, salted to keep and variously spiced. Fruit juices, above all green walnut, and shellfish juices from oysters and mussels also serve as bases. Common use, though, keeps the name for the mushroom kind.
britannica-1911-llandeilo-group:
Llandeilo Group is the middle layer of the Ordovician rocks of Britain, as a 1911 Britannica entry explains. Murchison first set out and named it from the town of Llandeilo in Carmarthenshire. In that home ground it holds slate, shale, lime rich flags, and sandstone beds. A lime rich middle bed is often called the Llandeilo limestone by field men.

Fierce volcanic action marks its tale in North Wales and Cumberland most of all. Great piles of lava and ash form hills such as Cader Idris today. The bed runs about two thousand feet thick in Wales on average measure. It is split in that ground into three parts for mapping work.
britannica-1911-llandovery-group:
Llandovery Group, a set of rock layers in Britain, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the lowest division of the Silurian system in Britain. A scholar in 1879 proposed the name Valentian for the group, from an old province of north Britain. In its home ground the group holds shales more than a thousand feet thick, plus sandstones above and below.

The article describes the lower rocks as gravels, sandstones, and slaty beds. At Llandovery they rest unevenly on older Ordovician rocks, though in many places no break can be traced. The layers run in a narrow band through Pembrokeshire and thin out northward. A change in the fossil life marks the step from the older system into this one. Among the graptolites, one family begins to give way to another, and their zones mark the beds in order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dupanloup:
Dupanloup, bishop of Orleans, was born at Saint-Felix in Savoy on 2 June 1802 and died at Lacombe on 11 October 1878. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his mother Anne Dechosal, to whom he stayed tenderly devoted, schooled him early. To shield his future from the shame of his illegitimate birth, she took him at seven to Paris. There, by work and privation, she kept him for a time at the College Sainte-Barbe.

After trials in other paths he chose the priesthood, studying at Saint-Nicolas, Issy, and Saint-Sulpice. Ordained on 18 December 1825, he served at the Madeleine, where he founded the famous catechisms of the Assumption. The entry follows him through the schools and councils of France to his place among the great bishops of his age.
doe-osti-3009666-trust-sensors-in-enviro:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-32167, by Grant Rydquist, John Blessinger, Peter Beck, and Samantha Ceballes, dated December 2025, reports fiscal 2025 work on the TRUST thermocouple testbed. The testbed asks how temperature sensors behave inside harsh thermal environments.

Airflow characterization tests probed the thermal chamber's air, and hard lessons about anemometer behaviour came with them. On the analysis side, a computational fluid dynamics capability was built from scratch for the chamber. The in-house Quinoa solver was tried first, but the team settled on a high-fidelity Fluent model as necessary for accurate results. The work feeds weapons-relevant thermal testing across the laboratory.
doe-osti-3011442-sustainable-tire-produc: Used tires become feedstock for new tires in a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory abstract, PNNL-37950, by Vanessa and Robert Dagle under CRADA 636. Bridgestone targets 100 percent sustainable materials by 2050 and is developing an end of life recycling route. Gasified tires yield syngas, which converts to ethanol by mature technology. Patented PNNL thermocatalytic technology then upgrades the ethanol into butadiene, a key tire precursor. The hosted record is the project abstract only, with no operating data.
doe-osti-3369030-deflagration-to-detonat:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21870, by Michael Hobbs, extends Sandia's deflagration-to-detonation work with XTIV, a pipeline that follows an explosive from first insult to final outcome. Earlier codes started mid-story. XTIV couples XCHEM, which models slow heating before ignition, to XDDT, which models the burn's possible turn into detonation. A cookoff in a fire can be simulated end to end, benign burst or catastrophe.

The handoff is the technical heart: XCHEM's state at thermal runaway crosses into XDDT through a single-timestep transfer file. Two schemas were built, one carrying pressure explicitly and one dropping it. A workable ignition threshold emerged near 800 kelvin for the slow-cookoff cylinder studied, just under the handoff gas peak of 807 kelvin. June 2026 printing.
doe-osti-3376035-unattended-monitoring-o:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-87790, dated September 2025, tests a slim sensor for watching uranium build up inside fuel reprocessing gear. Seven authors share the work, led by David L. Chichester, Jay D. Hix, and James T. Johnson. The sponsor was the Office of International Nuclear Safeguards. Holdup, the uranium that sticks in pipes and filters, is hard to tally from outside. A sensor that lives in place and reports on its own would aid safeguards checks.

The sensor is a scintillating fiber, under one centimeter thick in its rugged case. It flashes faintly when radiation hits, and a plain optical fiber carries the light away. Runs can stretch for kilometers to a safe control room. Bench work tied each head to a twenty-meter fiber reel and a LabVIEW screen. A final test showed the array catching nuclear material on the move inside a test facility.
doe-osti-3376726-schiff-moment-of-sup-12: Los Alamos National Laboratory slide set LA-UR-26-25428, issued July 1, 2026, by Ionel Stetcu, is a short progress note on computing Schiff moments for xenon-129 and mercury-199. The slides are sparse, mostly one summary block and a validation figure. Schiff moments gauge how a nucleus would react to forces that break time symmetry. The work ran on the Chicoma machine in 2025, using density functional theory extended to polarized odd nuclei. Dipole-push test runs showed no odd-system shift, as expected, but the same machinery is what Schiff moment work needs.
doe-osti-3382437-possible-paths-for-the-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-26175, issued July 21, 2026, weighs ways to produce arsenic-73. Seven authors are printed: Rene Reifarth, Aaron Joseph Couture, Hye Young Lee, Ellen Margaret O'Brien, Thanos Stamatopoulos, Etienne Vermeulen, and Jack Winkelbauer. The paper inside is dated June 3, 2026. Arsenic-73 is needed as a sample for nuclear reaction measurements. Such measurements are hard to make on radioactive nuclei.

The introduction explains why. Inelastic scattering reactions, including (n,2n), are rarely measured on radioactive targets. Signal gammas and neutrons hide in elastically scattered background. Three production paths are detailed. One uses selenium-74 with a proton beam. One uses germanium-72 with protons. One uses germanium-70 with alpha particles. Later chapters cover sample production and handling, gamma detection, and the DT facilities involved. Count rate estimates are given for each route.
doe-osti-3429343-physical-property-data-:
American Institute of Chemical Engineers closes award DE-EE0009768 with a final report on physical property data for organic acid separations. Julia Faeth led the project. The project ran from October 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025. Texas Tech, Argonne, and Siemens teams partnered on the work.

Models track how acids move through membranes as strength changes. Lactic and butyric acid behavior shifted with concentration in the tests. Acetic acid stayed nearly constant by contrast. The split is tied to Langmuir-type uptake in the membrane. Better property data help engineers design cheaper bio-based chemical plants.
doe-osti-3674463-how-distributed-energy-:
A slide deck by Ian Baring-Gould of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated July 14, 2026, explains how local energy resources can back up utility distribution networks. Distributed energy resources sit near customers and can supply part or all of local needs. The deck lists diesel, gas, and propane generators, solar panels, wind, combined heat and power, storage, demand response, and electric vehicles.

Three placement types are set out: behind the meter at a home or farm, front of the meter on local lines, and off-grid. Resilience options go beyond hardening poles and wires. They include spreading generation out, building resilience hubs, and forming microgrids that can island from the main grid. One slide maps hazard tools, from covered conductor and cameras to public safety power shutoffs. A later section shows H2Integrate, which times battery charging to cut peaks during grid stress for rural co-ops.
five-little-peppers-grown-up:
Margaret Sidney's Five Little Peppers Grown Up follows Polly, Phronsie, Joel and their family into adult life. Polly gives music lessons, the family prepares for Christmas at Dunraven, and festivities, bad news and many things in between test their bonds.

Later chapters bring Phronsie with a plan, Polly looking out for Charlotte, a recital, an accident, a farmhouse hospital, and Jasper's affairs. Mr. King attends to matters, Mother Fisher and Charlotte set things straight, and the book closes with home itself. Readers who grew up with the little brown house will find the grown-up Peppers faithful to their childhood selves.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Frame-Up_Frame-:
Harold Weisberg drafted a manuscript called Frame-Up to answer a critic. Robert Andrews had used a Washington Post Outlook piece to promote his book Death in a Promised Land. In Weisberg's view, the piece attacked his own work, and the manuscript answers back at length.

Weisberg defends his seven books on the Kennedy and King assassinations against charges of factual ignorance. The manuscript is a researcher protecting his life's work in public print terms. It preserves the feud whole, showing how personal the battles over the assassination record became. The piece survives as a manuscript among his papers, the draft of a public answer.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nato-75-: In December 1994, at a meeting in Budapest, the argument over NATO enlargement broke into the open between Washington and Moscow. Russian president Boris Yeltsin publicly accused the West of plunging Europe into a cold peace. This briefing-book page presents the record of that blow up, an early warning of the grievance that later defined Russian policy. The evidence here is the title alone, so the specific documents cannot be listed. The page marks the moment enlargement stopped being a quiet plan.
nasa-tm-19680004141-the-effects-of-the-g:
Bernard Kaufman, of the Mission and Trajectory Analysis Division at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in September 1967. It studies the effects of the Galilean moons on Jupiter flyby trajectories. A spacecraft swinging past Jupiter feels the gravity of its four big moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. It also feels the planet's own pull.

Kaufman integrated the equations of motion numerically for twenty different encounter trajectories, using an accurate model of the moons' motions. The moons' perturbations, he found, shift the spacecraft's post-encounter path around the Sun by amounts large enough to matter. Any detailed flyby study must therefore include the moons in its calculations. Broad mission measures, such as the travel time out to ten astronomical units, were little affected. A valuable by-product was a newly programmed ephemeris, a position table for the Galilean moons, not previously available in this country.
nasa-tm-19680014426-tankage-systems-for-:
Joseph D. Eisenberg and Rene E. Chambellan of Lewis Research Center studied fuel tanks for a methane fueled supersonic transport in this May 1968 report. Liquid methane could cut fuel costs for such an aircraft. Its very cold, cryogenic nature makes storage on board a hard design problem.

Fuel loaded in a saturated state would flash off as pressure drops during climb. Pressurized tanks or subcooled fuel can solve that problem instead. Subcooled fuel needs a pressurizing gas to push it out. The authors weigh gas choices, bladders, and standpipes that limit contact between gas and fuel. Their analysis compares these methods used alone and in combination.
nasa-tm-19710001519-reexamination-of-hea:
Peter M. Sockol and Ralph Forman of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1970 conference in Miami, Florida. It takes a fresh look at how a heat pipe starts up. A heat pipe moves heat along its length with almost no temperature drop.

Their test pipe used lithium and ran hot enough to glow. At such heat, the warming pattern can be seen as the pipe starts, they note. They check Cotter's standard model of startup against what they saw. Their revised model moves one key point and adds wall friction and condensation effects. Short-term readings tracked the pipe as it climbed to full heat.
pollyanna-grows-up:
Eleanor H. Porter followed her bestseller with Pollyanna Grows Up, billed on its title page as the Second Glad Book, illustrated by H. Weston Taylor and dedicated to her cousin Walter. The sequel sends the older Pollyanna to Boston, where her Aunt Polly's friend Mrs. Carew, a wealthy widow soured by the loss of a nephew, needs a dose of Pollyanna as badly as any patient in the first book. Contents promise some old friends at once, then new acquaintances: Jamie, a lame boy in Murphy's Alley who loves books and may be the lost nephew himself.

Jimmy Bean returns, grown and jealous, Aunt Polly takes alarm, and Pollyanna spends a stretch tied to two sticks after another accident before the game wins again. Porter knew exactly what her readers wanted: the same medicine, a larger dose, and a wedding at the end of it.
punky-dunk-and-the-spotted-pup:
Punky Dunk and the Spotted Pup is a rhyming picture book for young children, published in the shop of P. F. Volland and Company, Chicago, with a 1912 copyright. Its title page names no author and leaves space for the name of the good little child the story and pictures were made for.

On a day in the middle of May, Punky Dunk the cat watches a blue wagon back up to the sidewalk. The driver brings a heavy crate holding a gay spotted pup, white all over except for black spots on his back, tail, ears, and legs. Punky feels hurt, and calls the pup too fat to run or climb a tree.
ride-a-cock-horse-to-banbury-cross-a-far:
R. Caldecott's Picture Books present two nursery rhymes in this volume from Frederick Warne and Company. The first rhyme is printed verse by verse among its pictures: Ride a cock-horse to Banbury Cross. Its fine lady rides a white horse, to see what the rhyme promises.

Rings on her fingers and bells on her toes follow in the lines shown, the start of the old jingle. The second rhyme, named on the cover, tells of a farmer who went trotting upon his grey mare. Picture markers fill the pages between short lines, in the large, clear style made for young children hearing rhymes aloud.
the-aeroplane-boys-flight-or-a-hydroplan: John Luther Langworthy wrote The Aeroplane Boys Flight, or A Hydroplane Roundup, printed by M. A. Donohue and Company of Chicago and New York in 1914. Chapters listed run from The Boy Fliers and On Guard through The Air Scouts, Just Below the Clouds, The Pilot of the Mermaid, and A Clue to When Casper Came Back.
the-big-town-round-up:
William MacLeod Raine published a western novel in 1920, with a frontispiece by George Giguere. Chapter one concerns a street twelve miles long and opens on a cattle camp. Red Hollister grumbles that he likes the outfit and its cook, but not its meal hours.

For weeks Hollister has risen at three in the morning, eaten a hurried breakfast by a camp fire, and ridden after cattle wild as deer. He wrestles steers until after stars rise, then eats again near midnight. Raine, also named for A Man Four-Square and The Sheriff's Son, grounds big-town action in tired cow work first.
the-brimming-cup: Dorothy Canfield wrote The Brimming Cup, put out in New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1919. The list of parts starts with a Prelude and an Interlude. Part One then brings Old Mr. Welles and Young Mr. Marsh on stage. Table Talk and A Little Girl and Her Mother come next. Things Take Their Course leads to The Night-Blooming Cereus. What Goes On Inside is the last head shown. No page of the tale itself is given here.
the-frame-up:
Richard Harding Davis wrote The Frame Up as a tale of murder and city politics, opening with a phone call that promises a killer's name. District Attorney Wharton takes the call at lunch in Delmonico's.

Wharton lunches with a senator at the call of his brother-in-law, Hamilton Cutler, a power in the party who has held cabinet posts and charmed foreign courts. Davis draws the Cutler clan as the state's first family, rich and proud. Against that shine stands a county lawyer who owes his rise to his own work. A framed charge and a dead man named Banf pull both worlds into court.
the-letters-of-lord-nelson-to-lady-hamil:
Lord Nelson private letters to Lady Hamilton appeared in London in 1814, nine years after his death at Trafalgar. An advertisement explains why the editors added no notes to so well known an attachment. Some passages, they admit, were suppressed out of regard for living people who might feel pain.

Volume one also carries a supplement of letters by other distinguished people. The editors claim the letters show the great naval commander private merits without decoration. Readers get an early, guarded glimpse of a famous love affair, shaped by editors who cut as they printed.
the-queen-s-cup:
G. A. Henty opens at Greendale, Sir John Greendale's old mansion, where guests back from shooting talk at dusk about the Italian evil eye. Sixteen-year-old Bertha asks Captain Mallett whether he believes in the Mal Occhio.

Mallett answers carefully, saying one man has always stood between him and success. He recalls a school fight with a bully that proved far tougher than expected and counts it his only win over that rival. The fireside confession sets up a story of long rivalry and ill luck, told to a country-house audience on the first evening of the visit.
